name: Liquefaction Resonance Cannon LRC-3 'Mudmaker'
description: The LRC-3 'Mudmaker' is a heavy crew-served weapon that generates a sustained resonance field capable of inducing thixotropic liquefaction in granular and semi-solid substrates — effectively turning compacted soil, concrete aggregate, sand, gravel, and certain composite construction materials into a viscous slurry state for as long as the field is maintained. The weapon operates by broadcasting layered mechanical resonance waves from a parabolic emitter array, overwhelming the cohesive friction bonds between substrate particles and causing the material to behave as a liquid under applied stress. The effect is temporary — substrates re-solidify within sixty to ninety seconds of field termination — but the tactical implications of turning a floor, embankment, or fortified position into quicksand are considerable.
specifications: weight: 28 kg (emitter array + crew frame), 18 kg (capacitor backpack) crew: 2 (operator + power manager) effective range: 35 m (liquefaction field projection) field diameter: 4 m at maximum range (adjustable 1–4 m) liquefaction depth: Up to 1.2 m substrate penetration field maintenance duration: Continuous while powered; capacitor supports 40 seconds sustained operation re-solidification time: 60–90 seconds post-field termination compatible substrates: Compacted soil, sand, gravel, concrete aggregate, clay, certain composite materials incompatible substrates: Solid rock, reinforced synthcrete panels, metal decking power source: Dedicated resonance capacitor backpack (single-charge, field-rechargeable)
tactical_use: The 'Mudmaker' excels in siege and denial scenarios in earthwork or mixed-construction environments. Standard doctrine calls for liquefying approach corridors to immobilize advancing forces, collapsing tunnel sections to cut off retreat, or destabilizing the foundation substrate beneath fortified positions. The 'casting' effect — trapping targets in re-solidified material — is used deliberately in capture operations when targets need to be taken alive and immobile. Operators must account for the weapon's own weight and the risk of liquefying substrate beneath their own position; field accidents involving crew sinkage are common enough to have generated their own safety protocols.
cultural_context: The 'Mudmaker' has a cult following among GLMZ's tunnel-runner and underground infrastructure communities, where it is seen as a symbol of the blurred line between construction and destruction that defines the city's lower districts. Palladian Construction's involvement in its creation is considered an open secret — the company's logo appears on early-production emitter arrays, poorly obscured by aftermarket paint. Workers in GLMZ's extensive below-grade maintenance network tell stories about 'Mudmaker accidents' that are widely understood to be deliberate acts of labor sabotage against corporate infrastructure teams. The weapon is rarely seen above ground.
known_users: Corporate sabotage specialists targeting competitor infrastructure
Ouroboros Energy subsurface security teams (pipeline protection)
story_hooks: A section of GLMZ's primary transit tunnel has collapsed — official reports cite structural failure, but the substrate shows signs of resonance liquefaction. Someone used a 'Mudmaker' on a load-bearing section, and the city wants answers before more tunnels go down.

A Palladian Construction executive is trying to quietly buy back all existing 'Mudmaker' units on the black market before a regulatory audit connects the weapon's design to the company. They're paying well — but they're also eliminating sellers after the transaction.

The players need to breach a fortified underground compound. A contact offers them access to a 'Mudmaker' — but the power capacitor is damaged, and the only person who can repair it is currently trapped inside the compound they need to breach.

A 'Mudmaker' has been modified to operate at a resonance frequency that affects reinforced synthcrete — something Palladian Construction claimed was impossible. Someone has solved the incompatibility problem, and the implications for GLMZ's infrastructure are catastrophic.

physical_description.visual_profile: A heavy, asymmetrical crew-served apparatus dominated by a large parabolic dish emitter mounted on a stabilized tripod frame. The dish is the visual anchor—a wide, shallow satellite-dish-like structure bristling with concentric resonance rings. The operator's station sits forward of the emitter on a reinforced polymer mounting plate, with a grip assembly and targeting interface. A separate backpack power unit completes the system.
physical_description.dimensions: Emitter array: 140 cm height (mounted), 110 cm dish diameter. Operator frame: 85 cm length, 45 cm width. Capacitor backpack: 55 cm height × 30 cm width × 20 cm depth. Total footprint when operational: roughly 2 meters forward to back.
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and deliberate. The emitter assembly feels solid and grounded—designed to anchor against its own resonance output. The operator frame is balanced but muscular. The capacitor backpack is genuinely heavy (18 kg), requiring both shoulder straps and a waist support frame. Not a weapon for solo operation.
physical_description.primary_material: Steel load-bearing frame reinforced with carbon-composite struts. Parabolic emitter dish is fabricated from resonance-dampening aluminum alloy to focus wave propagation. Operator interface is rubberized polymer over a hardened steel skeleton. Capacitor backpack housing is brushed titanium.
physical_description.finish: Industrial and worn. The steel frame shows a dull gunmetal finish with light surface oxidation in high-stress areas. The parabolic dish has a brushed, almost granular appearance—residue buildup from substrate contact. The operator grips are heavily scored from gloved hands. The capacitor backpack bears scuff marks and stress fractures in the titanium casing, suggesting field repairs.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary: Gunmetal gray and brushed titanium. Accents: Matte black polymer controls and cable routing. Faded safety orange warning bands on the dish perimeter. The capacitor backpack has a dull metallic bronze tint from oxidation.
physical_description.grip_texture: Operator grips are textured rubber with reinforced knuckle guards—aggressive, non-slip. The targeting interface is smooth polymer with tactile button detents. The backpack shoulder straps are wrapped in wear-resistant synthetic fabric with integrated padding.
distinctive_features: Parabolic resonance dish with visible concentric etching—each ring corresponds to a harmonic frequency layer
Array of six sub-emitter apertures arrayed around the primary dish centerline, small black tubes that emit the actual resonance waves
Twin stabilization struts that lock into place during operation, reducing recoil drift
Amber-colored indicator LEDs along the operator console—power state, field strength, substrate compatibility readout
Heat venting louvers on the capacitor backpack, arranged vertically along both flanks
Heavy cable bundle connecting operator interface to backpack, wrapped in protective braid with quick-disconnect couplings
Faint scorch marks and substrate residue deposits around the base of the emitter—visible evidence of field use
Recalibration dial on the dish assembly—mechanical adjustment for field diameter and frequency modulation
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION logo stamped in chrome on the backpack housing, flanked by a batch code and serial plate. A smaller resonance-frequency certification plate is affixed to the operator frame, partially worn. Warning symbols in a dozen languages are stenciled across the capacitor unit.
physical_description.condition_typical: Battle-worn but maintained. Field crews treating this as equipment know it must function under pressure—visible repairs, replaced cables, reinforced joint tape, but no major structural compromise. Substrate residue cakes the lower third of the parabolic dish and the stabilization struts. The operator interface shows heavy use: scratched screens, worn button labels.
